description: What controls how fast a reaction goes and how much product we get.
content_html:
Rate of Reaction

The rate of reaction tells you how quickly a reaction proceeds. It is calculated from:

$$\text{rate} = \frac{\text{quantity of reactant used or product formed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

The units of rate depend on how the quantity is measured. If you measure the volume of gas produced in cm³ over time in seconds, the rate has units of cm³/s. A common student error is to measure volume in cm³ but record time in minutes, and then forget to convert — always check your units match.

Key Fact

Rate of reaction can be increased by: raising temperature, increasing concentration (or pressure for gases), increasing surface area of solid reactants, or using a catalyst. Rate = quantity of reactant or product ÷ time.

Collision Theory

Collision theory explains why rate changes when conditions change. A reaction only occurs when particles: (1) collide with each other, and (2) have at least the activation energy. If either condition is not met, particles bounce off without reacting.

Each factor affects either the frequency of collisions or the proportion that have enough energy:

  • Temperature — raising temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more frequently, and a greater proportion exceed the activation energy.
  • Concentration / Pressure — more particles in a given volume means more frequent collisions.
  • Surface area — breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface, increasing the area available for collisions.
  • Catalyst — provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. More collisions now have sufficient energy to succeed. The catalyst is not used up and does not appear in the overall equation.

Three common methods to measure reaction rate:

  1. Gas collection — gas produced is collected in a gas syringe or over water in an inverted measuring cylinder. Volume is recorded at intervals.
  2. Mass loss — the reaction vessel sits on a balance; mass decreases as gas escapes. Mass is recorded at intervals.
  3. Colour/turbidity change — used for reactions that produce a precipitate or change colour. The “disappearing cross” experiment (sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid) measures the time for a cross beneath the flask to become invisible as sulfur precipitate forms. Rate = 1 ÷ time.

A reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid produces CO&sub2; gas. After 20 s, 30 cm³ of gas has been collected. After 40 s, 50 cm³. Calculate the mean rate between 20 s and 40 s.

Rate = change in volume ÷ change in time = (50 − 30) cm³ ÷ (40 − 20) s = 20 ÷ 20 = 1.0 cm³/s.

Note: the units are cm³/s because volume was measured in cm³ and time in seconds. If time had been measured in minutes, the rate would be 1.0 cm³/min — these are not the same value. Always match units before calculating.

Key Fact

Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway. More collisions have sufficient energy to succeed. The catalyst is not used up and does not appear in the overall equation.

Yield and Atom Economy

Percentage yield compares what you actually obtained to what you could theoretically obtain:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Yield is rarely 100%. Reasons include: the reaction may not go to completion, some product is lost in filtering or transferring, or a reversible reaction may not fully favour the products. In industry, maximising yield while controlling costs is a key challenge.

Atom economy measures how efficiently atoms from reactants end up in the desired product:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{\text{relative formula mass of desired product}}{\text{sum of relative formula masses of all products}} \times 100$$

A high atom economy means less waste. Addition reactions (where all reactants become one product) have 100% atom economy. Reactions that produce by-products have lower atom economy. Green chemistry aims to maximise atom economy to reduce waste and cost.

Consider the reaction: \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\). The desired product is CaO (\(M_r = 56\)). The by-product is CO&sub2; (\(M_r = 44\)). Total mass of products = 56 + 44 = 100. Atom economy = (56 ÷ 100) × 100 = 56%. This means 44% of the atom mass ends up as the waste gas CO&sub2;.

Why Yield and Rate Both Matter

In industry, the goal is not simply to achieve the fastest possible rate or the highest possible yield — it is to produce the most product economically over time. A reaction that runs very quickly but has a low yield may be less profitable than a slower reaction with a high yield, depending on the cost of raw materials and energy. Conversely, a reaction with a high theoretical yield but a very slow rate may not be commercially viable without a catalyst to speed it up.

Industrial chemists therefore optimise conditions to balance rate and yield together. For example, using a catalyst simultaneously increases rate (without reducing yield) while allowing lower temperatures — reducing energy costs. Recycling unreacted starting materials back into the reaction vessel can also improve the overall yield over time, even if the yield at any single pass is moderate. These economic and environmental factors make the design of industrial chemical processes genuinely complex, and they illustrate why chemistry has real-world importance beyond the laboratory.
exam_tip_html: Rate calculation questions frequently involve unit errors — always check whether time is in seconds or minutes before dividing. For graph questions, the gradient at any point represents the rate: a steeper gradient means a faster rate. In collision theory questions, you must link the factor to frequency of collisions or proportion with sufficient energy — not just say “particles collide more.” For atom economy, remember addition reactions give 100% because all atoms end up in a single product.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate of reaction = quantity of reactant or product ÷ time. Four factors increase rate: higher temperature, higher concentration (or pressure), greater surface area, or a catalyst — all explained by collision theory and the activation energy concept.
  • Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. Yield is rarely 100% due to incomplete reactions, product loss, or reversible reactions.
  • Atom economy = (\(M_r\) of desired product ÷ total \(M_r\) of all products) × 100. High atom economy means less waste; addition reactions have 100% atom economy.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of CO₂ collected. In the first 30 seconds, 45 cm³ of gas is collected. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over this time. Include units.
practice_questions.marks: Rate = 45 cm³ ÷ 30 s = 1.5 cm³/s (1 mark for correct calculation; 1 mark for correct units of cm³/s). Common error: giving cm³/min by forgetting to convert. Mastering: correct answer with units. Secure: correct answer. Developing: correct division but wrong units. Emerging: formula not applied.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using collision theory, how increasing the temperature increases the rate of a chemical reaction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy (1); they move faster, so collisions are more frequent (1); a greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ the activation energy, so more are successful (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points — frequency or proportion mentioned but not both. Emerging: 'particles collide more' without linking to kinetic energy or activation energy.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a catalyst and explain how it increases the rate of reaction without being used up.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up in the overall reaction (1); it provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy (1); more collisions have sufficient energy to succeed, so the rate increases; the catalyst participates in the mechanism but is regenerated and not consumed overall (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: A reaction to make a drug compound produces 4.2 g of the desired product. The theoretical maximum yield is 6.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks: Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 (1 mark for formula); = (4.2 ÷ 6.0) × 100 (1 mark for substitution); = 70% (1 mark for answer); a percentage yield less than 100% could be due to incomplete reaction, product lost during transfer, or because the reaction is reversible (1 mark for reason). Mastering: all four. Secure: correct calculation and one reason. Developing: correct formula, arithmetic error. Emerging: formula stated only.

practice_questions.text: Hydrogen is manufactured by the reaction: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂. The desired product is H₂ (Mr = 2). Calculate the atom economy for this reaction. (Mr: CO = 28; H₂ = 2)
practice_questions.marks: Total Mr of desired product: 3 × 2 = 6 (1); total Mr of all products: 28 + 6 = 34 (1); atom economy = (6 ÷ 34) × 100 = 17.6% (allow 18%) (1); this is a low atom economy because CO is a by-product — most atom mass ends up as waste (1). Mastering: all four. Secure: correct calculation. Developing: formula applied but Mr sum incorrect. Emerging: formula stated only.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the effect of concentration on the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid using the disappearing cross method. Describe what they would measure and how they would calculate the rate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: place a conical flask over a piece of paper with a cross drawn on it (1); add sodium thiosulfate solution to the flask, then add hydrochloric acid and start a timer (1); record the time (in seconds) for the cross to disappear as sulfur precipitate forms (1); rate = 1 ÷ time — a shorter time means a faster rate (1). Secure: all four steps. Developing: three steps. Emerging: two steps.

knowledge_checks.q: A student collects 60 cm³ of gas in 30 seconds. What is the mean rate of reaction?
How does a catalyst increase the rate of reaction?
options: It increases the temperature of the reaction
It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
It increases the concentration of reactants
It reduces the activation energy by heating reactants

knowledge_checks.q: In collision theory, a reaction can only occur when particles collide with at least the _____ energy.
Match each factor to its effect on collision frequency or energy.
right: Increases both collision frequency and the proportion with enough energy
Increases the number of particles per unit volume

flashcard_questions.q: What is the equation for rate of reaction?
flashcard_questions.a: Rate = quantity of reactant used or product formed ÷ time taken.

flashcard_questions.q: A reaction collects 90 cm³ of gas in 60 seconds. What is the rate in cm³/s?

flashcard_questions.a: The minimum energy colliding particles need to react successfully.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a catalyst increase reaction rate?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a catalyst not appear in the overall equation?
flashcard_questions.a: It is not used up — it is regenerated during the reaction.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three methods used to measure rate of reaction.
flashcard_questions.a: Gas collection, mass loss on a balance, and colour/turbidity change (disappearing cross).

flashcard_questions.q: Give one reason why percentage yield is rarely 100%.
flashcard_questions.a: Product is lost during filtering or transferring, or the reaction is incomplete.
The Mr of the desired product ÷ total Mr of all products × 100.

flashcard_questions.q: What atom economy does an addition reaction have, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: 100%, because all reactant atoms end up in the single product with no by-products.

flashcard_questions.q: How does increasing surface area increase reaction rate?
flashcard_questions.a: More surface is exposed, so collisions between reactant particles are more frequent.

flashcard_questions.q: What units should rate of reaction have if volume is in cm³ and time in seconds?

glossary_terms.definition: A measure of how quickly reactants are converted into products; calculated as quantity of reactant or product ÷ time.
The theory that a chemical reaction only occurs when particles collide with at least the activation energy and in the correct orientation.
The minimum amount of energy that colliding reactant particles need to react and form products.
A substance that increases the rate of reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy; it is not used up in the reaction.
The mass of product actually obtained as a percentage of the maximum theoretical yield; calculated as (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100.
The proportion of atom masses from reactants that end up in the desired product, expressed as a percentage; higher values indicate less waste.
